PEP 241 specifies that the Distutils sdist command writes package metadata to a file named PKG-INFO in the top directory of the source distribution.
PEP 314 specifies version 1.1 of the package metadata format, whose version 1.0 is specified in PEP 241.
Metadata version 1.2 (PEP 345) adds the optional fields Requires-Python, Requires-External, Requires-Dist, Provides-Dist and Obsoletes-Dist to make third-party packaging easier.
PEP 426 specifies a metadata version 2.0 that was never released; it proposed moving from a custom key-value file format to a JSON-compatible in-memory representation.
PEP 459 proposed standard metadata extensions, each independently versioned, so that changing an extension format would not require an update to the core packaging metadata.
PEP 566 describes the changes from core metadata version 1.2 to version 2.1 and makes the Core Metadata Specification reference document the canonical source for field specifications.
PEP 643 states that metadata consumers could not rely on the metadata in source distributions and had to run the costly PEP 517 build mechanism to obtain it.
PEP 639 adopts the SPDX license expression syntax for expressing a Python project's license.
PEP 753 deprecates the Home-page and Download-URL metadata fields in favor of Project-URL equivalents and sets conventions for normalizing Project-URL labels.
PEP 794 adds repeatable Import-Name and Import-Namespace core metadata fields, matching pyproject.toml keys, and introduces core metadata version 2.5.
PEP 808 permits a static portion of a dynamic metadata field in the pyproject.toml [project] table when the field is a table or array.
Under PEP 808, metadata version 2.6 allows mixed static and dynamic metadata in source distribution metadata.
PEP 819 states that differences between implementations of the email-header metadata format, including handling of encodings and line breaks, have caused numerous packaging bugs.
PEP 819 proposes JSON-encoded core metadata and wheel metadata files in Python packages.
PEP 771 proposes that one or more extras can be installed by default when none are given, and that an empty extras set requests a minimal installation.
PEP 386 proposed a new version comparison schema system in Distutils.
PEP 440 defines a scheme for identifying versions of Python distributions and declaring dependencies on versions, addressing limitations of the versioning approaches in PEP 345 and PEP 386.
PEP 508 specifies the language for describing a single dependency and leaves which kinds of dependencies to install, and when, to higher-level specifications.
PEP 496 states that environment markers, first specified in PEP 345 and extended in PEP 426, became insufficient by the release of Python 2.7.10 because they relied on simple lexical comparisons.
PEP 390 proposed describing a package's metadata in a setup.cfg section without using setup.py.
PEP 685 specifies how to normalize extra names for comparison so that tools neither fail to find an extra nor match an unexpected one.
PEP 516 proposed a programmatic build interface to decouple pip from its hard dependency on setuptools.

PEP 517 states that distutils and setuptools lack usable build-time dependency declaration, are difficult to extend, and are hard to replace because they provide the standard installation interface that users expect.
PEP 518 introduces a new configuration file in which packages declare their build dependencies, with the expectation that the same file will hold future configuration.
PEP 621 specifies how to write a project's core metadata in pyproject.toml for packaging tools to consume.
PEP 631 was accepted and merged into PEP 621.
PEP 633 proposed a way to write dependencies in pyproject.toml as an alternative to the PEP 508-based approach of PEP 631.
PEP 725 proposes an [external] table in pyproject.toml for a project's non-PyPI build and runtime dependencies.
PEP 735 stores requirements in pyproject.toml in a way that excludes them from every built distribution of the project.
PEP 660 describes a PEP 517-style method for installing packages in editable mode.
PEP 662 proposed editable installs by extending PEP 517 backend-frontend communication with virtual wheels.
PEP 650 states that Python package installers are not completely interoperable with each other.
PEP 665 proposed a requirements file that is exhaustive for the installation target and can be used across platforms for reproducibility.
PEP 751 defines a human-readable, machine-generated file format from which installers can work out what to install without dependency resolution at install time.
PEP 722 proposed a format for declaring third-party dependencies inside a single-file Python script.
PEP 723 specifies a metadata format embedded in single-file Python scripts for launchers, IDEs and other external tools.
PEP 425 defines three compatibility tags (implementation and language version, ABI, and platform) for built distributions, kept terse because they appear in filenames.
PEP 427 defines the wheel as a ZIP-format archive with a specially formatted file name and the .whl extension, containing a single distribution nearly as it would be installed.
PEP 491 describes the second version of the wheel built-package format.
PEP 625 standardizes the source distribution as a gzipped tar file with a specially formatted name and .tar.gz suffix, and leaves its contents to other specifications.
PEP 513 proposed the manylinux1 platform tag, limiting external dependencies to a standardized, restricted subset of the Linux kernel and core userspace ABI.
PEP 571 proposed the manylinux2010 platform tag to succeed the manylinux1 tag.
PEP 599 proposed the manylinux2014 platform tag to succeed the manylinux2010 tag.
PEP 600 proposes defining new manylinux tags without a PEP for each tag, so maintainers can adopt new tags faster and limited volunteer time is used better.
PEP 600 lists handling non-glibc-based platforms as a non-goal.
PEP 656 proposes a musllinux platform tag series for musl-based Linux installations that works like the perennial manylinux tags of PEP 600.
PEP 777 states that a fundamental obstacle to evolving the wheel specification has been the lack of a defined process for adding backwards-incompatible features.
PEP 777 states that earlier efforts to improve the wheel specification were deferred to focus on other packaging specifications.
PEP 778 proposes a LINKS metadata file for symlinks in wheels, which requires a new wheel major version.
PEP 780 adds a sys_abi_features environment marker so that dependencies can depend on ABI features of the interpreter.

PEP 817 states that platform compatibility tags cannot express hardware features such as GPU acceleration or CPU instruction sets, nor build-time choices such as the BLAS implementation a wheel was built against.
PEP 825 defines the data format for variant wheels, storing additional compatibility data inside the wheel and a human-readable variant label in the filename.
PEP 850 determines variant compatibility either from static compatibility lists in the variant metadata or by querying opt-in plugins.
AB 1890 required SDG&E to lower electric rates by 10% for residential and small commercial customers and then froze rate levels.
SDG&E recovered many of its transition costs about two years early, partly by selling its two San Diego power plants at higher than expected prices.
On 1 February 2001 a large coalition of customer groups was working to pass language in Senate bill SBX 27 to fix the ABX 1 provision that permits a ban on new direct access agreements.
The coalition's bill aimed to give DWR and the CPUC specific direction so that they could not use their discretion to make customer choice more difficult.

A manufacturers' group proposed defining DWR's stranded costs as costs DWR cannot reasonably avoid until its long-term power contracts expire, so that direct access load within DWR's short-term purchases would face no exit fee.
On 20 February 2001 the CPUC circulated a draft order implementing the AB 1X provision to suspend direct access, intending to vote on it at that week's Thursday meeting.
The February 2001 draft order gave parties 30 days to address how the Commission should implement the suspension of direct access.
CDWR has until 1 January 2003 to fill the utilities' short position.
A February 2001 internal proposal held that direct access should proceed as long as the unfilled part of the net short exceeds the direct access load.
Under that proposal the balance would be calculated weekly up to 1 September 2002, when direct access would definitely close.
At a 2 March 2001 meeting, the Senate staff proposal on direct access was rejected by the attendees, although it moved away from a complete prohibition of direct access.
The customer group asked DWR and the Department of Finance to accept an exit fee for customers switching to direct access only if DWR's signed power contracts would leave actual stranded costs.
The customer group also asked for an open season of free switching to direct access when demand exceeds DWR's firm contracts, retained generation and QF supply.
On 7 March 2001 the CPUC adopted language that it would not second-guess DWR purchases and would pass DWR costs through to customers.
The 7 March 2001 CPUC decision dropped the proposed language that would have stayed Commission action on implementing the direct access prohibition.
As of 7 March 2001 the CPUC had no proposal before it to implement the direct access prohibition and no near-term plan to do so.
Under Assembly bill AB 21X as of 22 March 2001, a customer could switch to direct access after the bill's effective date by paying an exit fee based on DWR's unavoidable costs.
AB 21X would let customers switch to direct access without limitation before its effective date and let existing direct access customers stay.
AB 21X would charge a re-entry fee for returning from direct access to bundled service unless 12 months' advance notice is given.
As of 12 April 2001 the CPUC had not clarified how its 3 cent rate increase would apply to past, present or future direct access customers.
According to an attorney consulted on 12 April 2001, no one was then sponsoring bills to resolve the situation of direct access.

An April 2001 internal estimate put CDWR's monthly purchase-cost reduction at $41 million (at portfolio cost) to $130 million (at market price) if 5% of commercial and industrial load switched to direct access.
The April 2001 savings estimate assumed that every kWh of commercial and industrial load switching to direct access reduces CDWR purchases one for one, that is, that CDWR fills 100% of the net short.
AB 18X, an emergency bill, would create a core/noncore split in electricity similar to the one in California's gas market.
In the core/noncore model pitched in May 2001, core customers keep utility generation, QFs and DWR contracts, while noncore customers take the short position and buy at market.
In that model both core and noncore customers pay for DWR's past purchases, spread over 15 years.
A May 2001 internal analysis held that the 3 cent surcharge applies only until the end of the AB 1890 rate freeze, which would end no later than 1 March 2002.
Commercial staff asked whether moving load to direct access at once, with no ability to return to utility service, would give customers a lasting exemption from the surcharge.
On 29 May 2001 one of the Governor's financial advisors reported that the legislative version of the core/noncore model can work if noncore customers can contract for power at $80/MWh.

The legislative version of the core/noncore plan would raise bond issuance to about $20 billion, against about $13 billion under the MOU, and the Governor's advisors doubted the market would absorb it.
DWR's signed power contracts had out clauses that would let them lapse if DWR's credit was not in place by July 2001.
As of 6 June 2001 a CPUC commissioner's draft decision, as then drafted, set the date after which customers lose the right to switch to an electric service provider, as ABX1-1 directed.
As of 6 June 2001 there were reportedly still three CPUC votes in support of direct access.
In June 2001 the CPUC stated that it did not intend to get ahead of legislative efforts on direct access and was operating in parallel with the Legislature.
Direct access was not to be voted on at the CPUC meeting of 14 June 2001.
On 21 June 2001 legal staff expected the CPUC to act on suspending direct access at its 28 June 2001 meeting, with enough votes for the decision.
Legal staff recommended that all new direct access contracts be signed by both the marketer and the customer no later than 30 June 2001.
Legal staff expected that a customer returned to utility service after 1 July 2001 could not later return to direct access and might pay a re-entry fee.
The CPUC decision on suspending direct access also contained a utility recommendation to suspend further negative CTC payments to marketers.
The proposed decision would order SCE not to make cash payments for the negative CTC credit, would apply the same to PG&E and SDG&E, and was unclear on whether the suspension was permanent.
Under that decision the marketer would hold a bill-credit receivable instead of a cash receivable, whose value could be obtained only by using the utilities' services.
On 26 June 2001 the CPUC's swing-vote commissioner said he would vote for suspending direct access unless the legislature acted or the administration changed its mind.
On 26 June 2001 two CPUC commissioners were pessimistic about their chances of reversing the order suspending direct access.

A 27 June 2001 internal view put a 75% probability on direct access customers who used utility service in January to June 2001 paying an exit fee equal to the difference between market price and utility rates in that period.
After the CPUC vote was delayed, the same author judged exit fees for retroactive costs even more likely.
On 3 July 2001 the CPUC delayed any action on suspending direct access until mid-August, reportedly at the request of DWR, the Department of Finance and the State Treasurer's Office.
On 5 July 2001 SBX 27 on direct access failed on the Senate floor 23-11, short of the 27 votes its urgency clause required.
The author of SBX 27 said the viability of direct access would be tied to the amount of power DWR purchased.
As of 8 July 2001 the DWR contracts remained a key impediment to any core/noncore deal.
As of 8 July 2001 legislation for a dedicated rate component to repay the state for DWR power purchases, de-linking the bonds from the DWR contracts, might be on a slower track than expected.
The CPUC approved Resolution E-3726 on a 5-0 vote at its 12 July 2001 meeting.
Resolution E-3726 states that a direct access customer returning to bundled service will not be exempt from the surcharge.
ABX 1 says the CPUC shall suspend direct access but gives no timeline or criteria for doing so.
Outside counsel advised in July 2001 that limiting direct access to the net short position could be argued to be within the CPUC President's existing authority.

A 30 July 2001 update said direct access could make a rescue of SoCal Edison more difficult and that California bond issuances may be in jeopardy as direct access becomes more popular with municipalities.
In April 2001 government affairs staff asked for 1-, 3- and 5-year all-in prices for large customers in order to understand what a core/noncore split would mean.

PEP 778 proposes a LINKS metadata file for symlinks in wheels, which requires a new wheel major version.
PEP 780 adds a sys_abi_features environment marker so that dependencies can depend on ABI features of the interpreter.

PEP 817 states that platform compatibility tags cannot express hardware features such as GPU acceleration or CPU instruction sets, nor build-time choices such as the BLAS implementation a wheel was built against.
PEP 825 defines the data format for variant wheels, storing additional compatibility data inside the wheel and a human-readable variant label in the filename.
PEP 850 determines variant compatibility either from static compatibility lists in the variant metadata or by querying opt-in plugins.
AB 1890 required SDG&E to lower electric rates by 10% for residential and small commercial customers and then froze rate levels.
SDG&E recovered many of its transition costs about two years early, partly by selling its two San Diego power plants at higher than expected prices.
On 1 February 2001 a large coalition of customer groups was working to pass language in Senate bill SBX 27 to fix the ABX 1 provision that permits a ban on new direct access agreements.
The coalition's bill aimed to give DWR and the CPUC specific direction so that they could not use their discretion to make customer choice more difficult.

A manufacturers' group proposed defining DWR's stranded costs as costs DWR cannot reasonably avoid until its long-term power contracts expire, so that direct access load within DWR's short-term purchases would face no exit fee.
On 20 February 2001 the CPUC circulated a draft order implementing the AB 1X provision to suspend direct access, intending to vote on it at that week's Thursday meeting.
The February 2001 draft order gave parties 30 days to address how the Commission should implement the suspension of direct access.
CDWR has until 1 January 2003 to fill the utilities' short position.
A February 2001 internal proposal held that direct access should proceed as long as the unfilled part of the net short exceeds the direct access load.
Under that proposal the balance would be calculated weekly up to 1 September 2002, when direct access would definitely close.
At a 2 March 2001 meeting, the Senate staff proposal on direct access was rejected by the attendees, although it moved away from a complete prohibition of direct access.
The customer group asked DWR and the Department of Finance to accept an exit fee for customers switching to direct access only if DWR's signed power contracts would leave actual stranded costs.
The customer group also asked for an open season of free switching to direct access when demand exceeds DWR's firm contracts, retained generation and QF supply.
On 7 March 2001 the CPUC adopted language that it would not second-guess DWR purchases and would pass DWR costs through to customers.
The 7 March 2001 CPUC decision dropped the proposed language that would have stayed Commission action on implementing the direct access prohibition.
As of 7 March 2001 the CPUC had no proposal before it to implement the direct access prohibition and no near-term plan to do so.
Under Assembly bill AB 21X as of 22 March 2001, a customer could switch to direct access after the bill's effective date by paying an exit fee based on DWR's unavoidable costs.
AB 21X would let customers switch to direct access without limitation before its effective date and let existing direct access customers stay.
AB 21X would charge a re-entry fee for returning from direct access to bundled service unless 12 months' advance notice is given.
As of 12 April 2001 the CPUC had not clarified how its 3 cent rate increase would apply to past, present or future direct access customers.
According to an attorney consulted on 12 April 2001, no one was then sponsoring bills to resolve the situation of direct access.

An April 2001 internal estimate put CDWR's monthly purchase-cost reduction at $41 million (at portfolio cost) to $130 million (at market price) if 5% of commercial and industrial load switched to direct access.
The April 2001 savings estimate assumed that every kWh of commercial and industrial load switching to direct access reduces CDWR purchases one for one, that is, that CDWR fills 100% of the net short.
AB 18X, an emergency bill, would create a core/noncore split in electricity similar to the one in California's gas market.
In the core/noncore model pitched in May 2001, core customers keep utility generation, QFs and DWR contracts, while noncore customers take the short position and buy at market.
In that model both core and noncore customers pay for DWR's past purchases, spread over 15 years.
A May 2001 internal analysis held that the 3 cent surcharge applies only until the end of the AB 1890 rate freeze, which would end no later than 1 March 2002.
Commercial staff asked whether moving load to direct access at once, with no ability to return to utility service, would give customers a lasting exemption from the surcharge.
On 29 May 2001 one of the Governor's financial advisors reported that the legislative version of the core/noncore model can work if noncore customers can contract for power at $80/MWh.

The legislative version of the core/noncore plan would raise bond issuance to about $20 billion, against about $13 billion under the MOU, and the Governor's advisors doubted the market would absorb it.
DWR's signed power contracts had out clauses that would let them lapse if DWR's credit was not in place by July 2001.
As of 6 June 2001 a CPUC commissioner's draft decision, as then drafted, set the date after which customers lose the right to switch to an electric service provider, as ABX1-1 directed.
As of 6 June 2001 there were reportedly still three CPUC votes in support of direct access.
In June 2001 the CPUC stated that it did not intend to get ahead of legislative efforts on direct access and was operating in parallel with the Legislature.
Direct access was not to be voted on at the CPUC meeting of 14 June 2001.
On 21 June 2001 legal staff expected the CPUC to act on suspending direct access at its 28 June 2001 meeting, with enough votes for the decision.
Legal staff recommended that all new direct access contracts be signed by both the marketer and the customer no later than 30 June 2001.
Legal staff expected that a customer returned to utility service after 1 July 2001 could not later return to direct access and might pay a re-entry fee.
The CPUC decision on suspending direct access also contained a utility recommendation to suspend further negative CTC payments to marketers.
The proposed decision would order SCE not to make cash payments for the negative CTC credit, would apply the same to PG&E and SDG&E, and was unclear on whether the suspension was permanent.
Under that decision the marketer would hold a bill-credit receivable instead of a cash receivable, whose value could be obtained only by using the utilities' services.
On 26 June 2001 the CPUC's swing-vote commissioner said he would vote for suspending direct access unless the legislature acted or the administration changed its mind.
On 26 June 2001 two CPUC commissioners were pessimistic about their chances of reversing the order suspending direct access.

A 27 June 2001 internal view put a 75% probability on direct access customers who used utility service in January to June 2001 paying an exit fee equal to the difference between market price and utility rates in that period.
After the CPUC vote was delayed, the same author judged exit fees for retroactive costs even more likely.
On 3 July 2001 the CPUC delayed any action on suspending direct access until mid-August, reportedly at the request of DWR, the Department of Finance and the State Treasurer's Office.
On 5 July 2001 SBX 27 on direct access failed on the Senate floor 23-11, short of the 27 votes its urgency clause required.
The author of SBX 27 said the viability of direct access would be tied to the amount of power DWR purchased.
As of 8 July 2001 the DWR contracts remained a key impediment to any core/noncore deal.
As of 8 July 2001 legislation for a dedicated rate component to repay the state for DWR power purchases, de-linking the bonds from the DWR contracts, might be on a slower track than expected.
The CPUC approved Resolution E-3726 on a 5-0 vote at its 12 July 2001 meeting.
Resolution E-3726 states that a direct access customer returning to bundled service will not be exempt from the surcharge.
ABX 1 says the CPUC shall suspend direct access but gives no timeline or criteria for doing so.
Outside counsel advised in July 2001 that limiting direct access to the net short position could be argued to be within the CPUC President's existing authority.

A 30 July 2001 update said direct access could make a rescue of SoCal Edison more difficult and that California bond issuances may be in jeopardy as direct access becomes more popular with municipalities.
In April 2001 government affairs staff asked for 1-, 3- and 5-year all-in prices for large customers in order to understand what a core/noncore split would mean.
